cues.text: Let us now turn to the case study and the lab exercises that close this study session.
Our case is MetroTech University.
The first thing to notice is the scale of the problem.
MetroTech has over six hundred users, and its network suffers from three weaknesses.
First, there is peak exam congestion, meaning the network becomes overloaded precisely when many people need it at once during examinations.
Second, the encryption is inadequate, so data is not protected as well as it should be.
Third, there is inadequate redundancy, meaning there are not enough backup paths or backup devices to keep the network running when something fails.
Now let us look at what the case proposes, and I will take the elements in the order the case gives them.
It proposes a star or hierarchical infrastructure.
It proposes department VLANs, that is, virtual local area networks, so that each department has its own logically separated network.
It proposes redundant core links, so the central part of the network has more than one connection.
It proposes load-balanced servers, where traffic is spread across several servers rather than landing on one.

It proposes firewalls to control traffic, VPNs, or virtual private networks, to protect traffic with encryption, an IDS, an intrusion detection system, to spot suspicious activity, and Zero Trust, the approach in which nothing is trusted automatically and access is verified.
Alongside all of this, the case proposes capacity upgrades and monitoring, so that there is more bandwidth and so that performance can be observed.
Two cautions come with this case, and both matter.
The first is that a single central switch without redundancy remains a failure point.
In a star design, everything connects through the centre.
If that one switch has no backup, then its failure takes the whole network down, so the design is only as strong as that central point unless redundancy is added.
The second caution concerns testing.
You should test end-to-end portal dependencies.

That means checking the whole chain that the university portal relies on, from the user's connection through to the portal itself and everything it depends on, rather than assuming each piece works because it was installed.
Finally, the case reports improved performance.
But notice the careful wording of the source: do not assume all controls work without measured evidence.
A report of improvement does not prove that the firewalls, VPNs, IDS, Zero Trust measures and redundancy each work.
Each control needs to be confirmed by actual measurement.
Now to the labs, of which there are two.
The first is the capstone security lab.

It uses three tools: the pfSense stateful firewall, router ACLs, which are access control lists on the router, and Suricata, which acts as an IDS and also as an IPS, that is, an intrusion prevention system.
The steps run in this order.
First, define a source, destination and service matrix.
This is a table listing which source may reach which destination, and over which service.
Second, implement least privilege, meaning each flow is allowed only if it is actually needed, and everything else is denied.
Third, test a permitted HTTPS flow, which should succeed, and test a denied database flow and a denied management flow, which should be blocked.
Fourth, verify the logs and alerts, using benign lab traffic, which means harmless traffic generated only for the exercise.
The second is the IPsec and WPA3 connectivity lab.
Here you design site-to-site tunnels with authorised peers, meaning only approved devices at each end may establish the tunnel.
You use IKEv2, the Internet Key Exchange version 2, and you place the sites on separate subnets.
Then you verify four things: the tunnel status, the permitted traffic, failover, and wireless client isolation, where wireless clients are kept from communicating directly with one another.
One last and important point.
The source states that no live deployment or test result is claimed.
These labs describe what to design and what to verify.
They do not report that anyone has run them or what the results were, so any outcome must come from your own measured testing.
